title: How Boot decides which beans you get
summary: From @SpringBootApplication to a bean that exists or does not: candidates are read from a file, sorted, filtered, and then each one's conditions are evaluated twice - once for the class, once per @Bean method.
entry: Run any Boot application with --debug. The CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT it prints is the output of this path, and the fastest way to answer 'why is that bean not there'. Then put a breakpoint in SpringBootCondition.matches to watch one decision being made.

steps.notice: The BeanFactoryPostProcessor that drives all of this. Note when it runs: definitions only, no instances, which is why every condition is a question about definitions.
The first line asks the ConditionEvaluator whether to skip the whole class. A class-level condition that says no means the @Bean methods inside are never even read.
Forty lines that are the whole @Conditional mechanism. Note the phase argument, and that conditions are sorted by order before being asked.
Where the candidate list comes from: META-INF/spring/*.AutoConfiguration.imports on every jar. Open one from your own dependencies and read it - it is a plain list of class names.

Alphabetical, then @AutoConfigureOrder, then @AutoConfigureAfter/@AutoConfigureBefore. This sort is the only reason @ConditionalOnMissingBean gives a stable answer between two auto-configurations - and the reason it does not between two of your own @Configuration classes.

Exclusions, then the filters. AutoConfigurationImportFilter is the fast path: OnClassCondition checks the class names from the .imports file against the classpath before anything is parsed, which is what keeps startup quick with a hundred candidates.

The base class for every @ConditionalOnX. It calls getMatchOutcome and then records the result, which is exactly what --debug prints. Every Boot condition produces a human-readable reason, and that is a good pattern to copy in your own.
Two lines, and the reason @ConditionalOnMissingBean works at all: it declares REGISTER_BEAN, so it is evaluated when bean definitions are being registered rather than when the class is being parsed.
The second evaluation. Each @Bean method gets its own shouldSkip call, in the REGISTER_BEAN phase, against a bean factory that already holds everything registered before it.
